title: New Jersey chosen as World Cup base by Brazil, Morocco, Haiti, Senegal
content:
New Jersey will be the base camp for four teams during the FIFA World Cup this summer, with Morocco and Haiti joining Brazil and Senegal in the region.

According to sources familiar with the planning, Brazil, Haiti, Morocco, and Senegal have now all confirmed facilities in New Jersey for the tournament, with a formal announcement expected this week.

It makes the region one of the most in-demand for training bases across the co-hosts United States, Canada and Mexico this summer — rivaled only by Kansas City, whose training bases will house Argentina, England, the Netherlands and Algeria.

Brazil’s home will be the Columbia Park Training Center in Morris Township, New Jersey, which is the everyday home of MLS team New York Red Bulls and a newly improved 80-acre facility which cost in excess of $100million (£74m).

Brazil have a group stage game at MetLife Stadium, as well as a game relatively nearby in Philadelphia and then down the east coast in Miami.

Two of Brazil’s World Cup group stage opponents Morocco and Haiti will also join the 1994 World Cup winners in staying in the New Jersey area.

Morocco, who finished as semi-finalists at the World Cup in Qatar in 2022, will use Pingry School as their training base. Pingry was also a World Cup base camp on the previous occasion the U.S. hosted the tournament in 1994, when eventual finalists Italy chose to train there.

Haiti, meanwhile, will be based in Galloway, New Jersey — not too far from Atlantic City — at Stockton University. The campus hosted Brazilian side Flamengo during the FIFA Club World Cup last summer.

Senegal, the original winners of this year’s Africa Cup of Nations before competition organisers reversed the final result, complete the quartet and will train at Rutgers University. The nation have two group stage games scheduled at MetLife Stadium in the group phase, playing against France on June 16 and Norway on June 22.

The 2026 World Cup will conclude at MetLife Stadium, with the venue hosting the final on July 19.

For New Jersey and FIFA, it is a rare positive story about their partnership after a very public spat in recent weeks. Much of the airtime surrounding the region’s preparations has been consumed by New Jersey Transit’s decision to hike rail prices up to $150 for a return trip from New York Penn Station to MetLife Stadium during the World Cup.

That decision pitted FIFA against the New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill, who claimed that she was not prepared to ask the local taxpayer to take on a $48m cost to fund transportation services to the World Cup when FIFA is forecasting revenues in excess of $11billion during the tournament. FIFA responded by citing lower transportation prices in host cities across the countries and warned that the NJ Transit’s decision could have a “chilling” impact.

In a statement welcoming the four nations to New Jersey, Gov. Sherrill said her state is “excited to welcome the world.”

She added: “This is a once-in-a-generation event, and we are proud that New Jersey will be at the very center of the festivities, hosting not only millions of soccer fans but also four national teams that have chosen to make our state their base of operations for the duration of the tournament.

“We are thrilled that Brazil, Haiti, Morocco, and Senegal have decided to call the Garden State home, bringing the World Cup directly to communities across our state and driving economic activity throughout the region. Their decision underscores what we know to be true: New Jersey is a premier destination for world-class events and tourism.”
